intro.speaker: mira
intro.text: New case, detective. A paper claims it killed off recurrence and convolutions for good — using attention alone.

intro.speaker: summary
intro.text: Skip the reading. I'll just tell you: it's the best model ever, period.

intro.speaker: mira
intro.text: That's exactly the kind of line we're here to check.

boss.mechanicReason: Frame boss: confront the suspect's version of the Transformer's core claim and architecture.

item.speaker: summary
item.prompt: The Summary's take on why the Transformer matters. One claim overclaims — find the passage that limits it.

statements.text: The Transformer dispenses with recurrence and convolutions entirely, relying solely on attention.
statements.why: The abstract states this directly as the architecture's design.

sourceRefs.quote: dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely

statements.text: The encoder is built as a stack of six identical layers, each with self-attention and feed-forward sub-layers.
statements.why: This matches the described encoder construction.

sourceRefs.quote: The encoder is composed of a stack of N = 6 identical layers.

statements.text: Self-attention needs only a constant number of sequential operations, while recurrent layers need operations that grow with sequence length.
statements.why: Table 1 reports exactly this contrast between self-attention and recurrent layers.

statements.text: The paper proves the Transformer is superior across many NLP benchmarks.
statements.why: The experiments only cover two machine translation tasks, not a broad range of benchmarks — the claim goes beyond what was tested.

sourceRefs.quote: Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality

hints: Which claim talks about results the experiments section never actually tested?

outro.speaker: mira
outro.text: Case closed. The Transformer really does drop recurrence and convolutions — but 'superior across many benchmarks' was never on the record. Two translation tasks, that's it.

intro.speaker: mira
intro.text: This case is about the engine room: queries, keys, values, and how attention actually gets computed.

intro.speaker: summary
intro.text: Details, details. Dot-product wins, always. Trust me.

intro.speaker: mira
intro.text: We don't trust, we check sources.

boss.mechanicReason: Frame boss: test the suspect's claims about how scaled dot-product and multi-head attention actually work.

item.speaker: summary
item.prompt: The Summary's version of the attention mechanism. One claim overreaches — produce the passage that corrects it.

statements.text: Attention maps a query and key-value pairs to an output, where the weight on each value comes from a compatibility function between the query and the key.
statements.why: This is exactly how the attention function is defined.

sourceRefs.quote: the weight assigned to each value is computed by a compatibility function of the query with the corresponding key.

statements.text: Scaled dot-product attention divides the dot products by √dk before applying softmax.
statements.why: This matches the formula's second step exactly.

statements.text: Dot-product attention is faster and more space-efficient in practice than additive attention because it uses optimized matrix multiplication.
statements.why: The paper states this practical advantage directly.

sourceRefs.quote: dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice, since it can be implemented using highly optimized matrix multiplication code.

statements.text: Dot-product attention always outperforms additive attention, since it's the simpler mechanism.
statements.why: Without scaling, additive attention actually outperforms dot-product attention for larger values of dk — it does not always win.

sourceRefs.quote: additive attention outperforms dot product attention without scaling for larger values of dk

hints: Check what happens without scaling when dk gets large — does dot-product still win?

outro.speaker: mira
outro.text: The math holds up — dot-product attention is faster in practice. But 'always outperforms' doesn't survive cross-examination; the paper says additive wins for large dk without scaling.

intro.speaker: mira
intro.text: Final case: the results. State-of-the-art BLEU scores, some ablations, and a side-claim about interpretability.

intro.speaker: summary
intro.text: Record-breaking everywhere, no exceptions. Case basically solves itself.

intro.speaker: mira
intro.text: Let's see what the numbers actually say before you close the file.

boss.mechanicReason: Frame boss: separate the Transformer's proven results from the suspect's sweeping conclusions.

item.speaker: summary
item.prompt: The Summary's closing statement on the results. One claim overclaims — bring the passage that disproves it.

statements.text: The big Transformer set a new English-to-German state of the art of 28.4 BLEU, beating the previous best (including ensembles) by more than 2 BLEU.
statements.why: The results section reports exactly this score and margin.

sourceRefs.quote: the big transformer model (Transformer (big) in Table 2) outperforms the best previously reported models (including ensembles) by more than 2.0 BLEU, establishing a new state-of-the-art BLEU score of 28.4.

statements.text: The Transformer generalized well to English constituency parsing, even with only the small WSJ training set.
statements.why: This matches the paper's reported parsing results on limited data.

sourceRefs.quote: even when training only on the WSJ training set of 40K sentences.

statements.text: The paper only tentatively suggests self-attention could yield more interpretable models, based on discussing a few example attention patterns.
statements.why: The text hedges with 'could yield' and points to examples in the appendix, not a full proof.

sourceRefs.quote: As side benefit, self-attention could yield more interpretable models.
We inspect attention distributions from our models and present and discuss examples in the appendix.

statements.text: The Transformer beat every previously reported parser, proving self-attention is best for all structured tasks.
statements.why: The paper explicitly reports one exception — the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar still scored higher — and never claims superiority for all structured tasks.

sourceRefs.quote: yielding better results than all previously reported models with the exception of the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar

hints: Check the parsing table — did the Transformer really beat every single prior model, with no exceptions?

outro.speaker: mira
outro.text: The BLEU numbers and the parsing generalization check out. But 'beat every parser, proving it's best for all structured tasks' falls apart — one model still scored higher, and the paper never claims universal superiority.
